etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English brewen, from Old English brēowan, from Proto-West Germanic *breuwan, from Proto-Germanic *brewwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁-. Doublet of burn.

Cognate with Dutch brouwen, German brauen, Swedish brygga, Norwegian Bokmål brygge; also Ancient Greek φρέαρ (phréar, “well”), Latin fervēre (“to be hot; to burn; to boil”), Old Irish bruth (“violent, boiling heat”), Sanskrit भुर्वन् (bhurván, “motion of water”). It may be related to English barley

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To make tea or coffee by mixing tea leaves or coffee beans with hot water.

quote.citation: 1935, Christopher Isherwood, chapter 11, in Mr Norris Changes Trains, Penguin, published 1942, page 113:
quote.text: Elderly people sat indoors, in the damp. shabby houses, brewing malt coffee or weak tea and talking without animation  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To heat wine, infusing it with spices; to mull.

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merry Wiues of Windsor”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene v]:
quote.text: Go, brew me a pottle of sack finely.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To make a hot soup by combining ingredients and boiling them in water.
(transitive, intransitive) To make beer by steeping a starch source in water and fermenting the resulting sweet liquid with yeast.
(transitive) To foment or prepare, as by brewing

quote.citation: 1634 October 9 (first performance), [John Milton], edited by H[enry] Lawes, A Maske Presented at Ludlow Castle, 1634: […] [Comus], London:  […]  [Augustine Matthews] for Hvmphrey Robinson, […], published 1637, →OCLC; reprinted as Comus: […] (Dodd, Mead & Company’s Facsimile Reprints of Rare Books; Literature Series; no. I), New York, N.Y.: Dodd, Mead & Company, 1903, →OCLC, page 106:
quote.text: Hence with thy brew’d inchantments, foul deceiver  […]

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To attend to the business, or go through the processes, of brewing or making beer.

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merry Wiues of Windsor”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iv]:
quote.text: I wash, wring, brew, bake, scour, dress meat and drink  […]

definitions.definition: (intransitive, of an unwelcome event) To be in a state of preparation; to be mixing, forming, or gathering.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene v]:
quote.text: There is some ill a-brewing towards my rest,

quote.citation: 2004 October 29, Marco R. Della Cava, “Vaccine shortage pricks tempers”, in Statesman Journal, volume 152, number 214, Salem, OR, page 2A:
quote.text: Of course, no one knows what kind of flu season is brewing, the perfect storm of a new strain hitting a largely unvaccinated population or a mercifully mild few months.

quote.citation: 2011 January 11, Jonathan Stevenson, “West Ham 2 - 1 Birmingham”, in BBC‎[1]:
quote.text: Grant may have considered that only a performance of the very highest quality could keep him in a job - and the way his players started the game gave the 55-year-old shelter from the storm that was brewing.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To boil or seethe; to cook.

quote.citation: 1886, Peter Christen Asbjørnsen, translated by H.L. Brækstad, Folk and Fairy Tales, page 6:
quote.text: She had one day to get up very early in the morning to brew, when the other servants said to her: 'You had better mind you don't get up too early, and you mustn't put any fire under the copper before two o'clock.'

quote.citation: 2007 March 6, Julie Rutterford, Life on Mars, Season 2, Episode 3:
quote.text: Landlady: You're not stoppin' for a brew?Gene Hunt: No thanks, love. Better crack on.

definitions.definition: The mixture formed by brewing; that which is brewed; a brewage, such as tea or beer.

quote.citation: 1959, Anthony Burgess, Beds in the East (The Malayan Trilogy), published 1972, page 529:
quote.text: Six great bottles of one of the Hong Kong brews had been brought to wash down the brandy and the fragments of rice and mee and meat-fibres that clung to the back teeth.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English brewe (“eyebrow”), from Old English bru (“eyebrow”). Doublet of brow.

definitions.definition: (British, dialect) An overhanging hill or cliff.
